already have been delivered and that its own earlier acknowledgement was lost; a

than a loss. QoS 2 buys the other promise — "exactly once" — and pays for it with
four packets and two round trips: PUBLISH, PUBREC, PUBREL, PUBCOMP. The message
itself travels in the first of them; the other three exist only so that both sides
can agree, without any doubt, that it arrived *and* that the handshake about it is
over.

That agreement is a state machine with an id in the middle of it, and every hard
part of this stage is about when that id may move. The sender's id is in flight
from the moment it is taken until the PUBCOMP — not until the PUBREC, not until
the PUBREL was written. The receiver holds both the id **and the message** from
the PUBLISH until the PUBREL, and it delivers the message at exactly one instant:
when the PUBREL arrives. Not at the PUBLISH — a receiver cannot tell a first
transmission from a re-send by looking at it, and a peer that reconnects may
re-send without the DUP bit set at all, so delivering on sight turns QoS 2 into
QoS 1 with two extra packets and a lie in its name. Not at the PUBREC either: the
receipt says "I have it", and the PUBREL says "I am done with this id" — the
message is released by the second of those, and by nothing else.

The two sides are therefore not symmetric, and this stage keeps them apart. A
`Sender` takes ids from stage 6's `PacketIds` (the stage that owns the rule that
an id in flight is not handed out again), records what it sent, and answers an
acknowledgement with the next body to write — `None` when the handshake is over.
A `Receiver` holds what it was told, acknowledges each PUBLISH including the
re-sends, and hands the message over once, when the PUBREL arrives. Both are
driven by the caller (stage 10), never by a poll: the tick is the caller's,
handed in with every packet it moves — `start`, `received` — and read by `due`,
which answers a record whose deadline has passed, one re-send per deadline, `DUP`
on a re-sent PUBLISH and never on a PUBREL.

    HANDSHAKE_KEYS   ("packet_id", "message", "state"): one delivery in flight, in order
    Sender(ids)          our side: take an id, PUBLISH, PUBREL, release at PUBCOMP

Everything so far has been about one connection. The session is the broker's
memory of a client that is not connected any more, and it exists because MQTT
makes four promises that a socket cannot keep on its own: the subscriptions a
client has made, the messages queued for it while it was away, the will it asked
to have published if it vanished, and the keep-alive it asked for — a number the
broker uses to decide, with no network help at all, that the connection is over.

closes the stream and leaves the record in place: the subscriptions are still in
force, and the messages for those subscriptions are still owed. A client that
comes back with a clean start of 0 is handed that record back, and everything it
had is true again **before** it sends its first SUBSCRIBE — a broker that waits
for the new SUBSCRIBE has already lost the messages published in the meantime.

old one is thrown away whole: subscriptions, queue and all.

The two promises that are *owed* rather than *kept* are the ones this stage has
to get exactly right. The queue is bounded by `QUEUE_MAX`, and a bounded queue
has to decide which end to drop: this one drops the newest, keeps the oldest,
and counts what it dropped in the session's `pending` field, because a message
that disappears without a count is the failure that is never noticed. And the
will is published only on an end the client did not choose — a `cut` or a
keep-alive expiry, never a DISCONNECT — and it leaves the session as it is
handed back, so an abnormal end cannot fire a promise a previous connection
already paid.

"""MQTT Broker From Scratch — stage 9: Grants, denials, and the line written before the act.

Every stage so far has read or written bytes. This one reads none, and that is
the point of it. What a client may publish and what it may subscribe to is not on
the wire: it is a table an operator wrote, and the wire hears almost nothing
about it. MQTT has no packet for "your PUBLISH was refused" — a broker that drops
it says nothing at all, and the client is free to believe it was delivered — and
the one thing a broker can say is a SUBACK whose code is the failure, which is
why a denial has to be a decision this broker wrote down rather than a packet it
sent.

So the decision is a line. It carries who asked, for what, when, and what the
answer was, in the fixed shape of the world's `DECISION_KEYS`: two decisions of
the same kind are then the same string, an audit can be counted without being
parsed, and a run can be compared with the run before it. Its reason comes from a
closed vocabulary — there are six words a refusal may use and no seventh — and
the line is written *before* the act it allows, which turns the interesting event
into a line with no act after it, and makes an act with no line impossible.

The judgment itself reads two tables together. The first is the client's own
grants, one list of patterns for publishing and one for subscribing, and the
request is matched against them by *components*: stage 3's matcher, never
`startswith`, so `a/b` does not reach `a/bc`, `+` is exactly one level, and `#` is
its own level and everything under it. The second is the broker's ceiling — the
widest reach any client may have — and it is not advice: a grant narrows the
ceiling and never widens it, so what a client may do is the intersection of the
two. A topic its grant reaches but the ceiling does not is refused, and so is one
the ceiling reaches and its grant does not.

    DECISION_KEYS                                  the six fields of a decision, in line order
    allowed_publish(grants, client_id, topic)      -> (allowed, reason)
    allowed_subscribe(grants, client_id, filter)   -> (allowed, reason)
    decide(grants, client_id, action, topic, tick) -> the decision the line is written from
    Ledger.before(decision)                        -> the line, written before the act it allows
    Ledger.lines()                                 -> the lines written, in order
    Ledger.denials()                               -> the decision dicts that refused
    Ledger.allowed()                               -> the decision dicts that allowed
    Ledger.report()                                -> {"lines", "allowed", "denied", "by-reason"}

The six reasons are the world's and not this stage's: `allowed`, `no-grant` (this
client has no grant that reaches here), `ceiling` (its grant does, and the
broker's own reach ends sooner), `wildcard` and `empty` (the request cannot be a
topic at all, and stage 3's `validate_topic` is the judge), and `malformed` (a
pattern in the table is not a filter, and `validate_filter` is the judge). What
this stage refuses instead of answering is a `grants.GrantsError`: a table that
is not a table, an action that is not an action, a tick that is not a tick. Note
that the table is handed in a parameter named `grants` — the contract's own
signature — so inside these functions that name is the table and not the module.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a client's power the intersection of its grants and the
broker's ceiling, rather than their union?
Because a policy that can only add is a policy with no top. The two tables answer
different questions — "may this client do this" and "may anyone do this here" —
and the safe reading of two walls is that you must fit through both. Unioned,
a single careless grant (`#` for one client, say) silently overrides the
ceiling for that client, and the ceiling stops being a ceiling exactly where it
was needed. Intersected, a grant can only take reach away, which is what makes a
narrow grant a safe thing to hand out and makes the ceiling worth writing down.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the client's own grant judged before the ceiling, and
the request's shape before both?
Because the reason a client is given should be the smallest true one. A client
whose grant does not reach the topic has no grant for it, whatever the ceiling
says, and telling it about the broker's ceiling would be answering a question it
did not ask. A request that could not be a topic in the first place — a wildcard,
an empty name — is refused before either table is consulted, because no grant
could make it legal. And a pattern in the table that could never be a filter is
judged before both, because a table nobody can read grants nothing.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a denial a returned verdict with a reason code, while a
table that is not a table raises?
Because one is content and the other is a shape. "May this client publish here"
is a question about the world, and this course answers questions with values —
the pair `(allowed, reason)`, or a decision dict — so a refusal never escapes as
an exception a caller might not expect to catch. A `Grants` table handed a
non-table, an action outside the two this protocol has, a tick that is not a
count: those are callers breaking the interface, and they raise, naming what
arrived. The reason itself is never free text, because the report counts by
reason and a seventh word would be a count nobody can compare.

DESIGN DECISION — why does the ledger write the line before the act, and hold the
decision rather than the text?
Because a line written afterwards can always be made to agree with what happened,
and then it is not evidence. `before` computes the line first — a decision the
world's `line` refuses is not recorded at all — and answers it, so at the moment
the caller performs the act the line is already on the ledger. The ledger holds a
copy of the decision and writes the line again on demand, so what a caller does
to its own dict afterwards cannot rewrite what was written: the line is the
evidence, and evidence that can be edited from outside is a diary.

DESIGN DECISION — why does a grant of `#` not reach a `$SYS/…` topic?
Because a grant is judged by stage 3's matcher, and that matcher keeps MQTT's
`$` rule: a filter whose first level is a wildcard does not reach a topic whose
first level begins with `$`. The rule exists so that a wildcard subscription does
not silently swallow the broker's own housekeeping tree, and a grant is a
subscription-shaped thing: a client granted `#` that could publish into
`$SYS/broker/uptime` would be able to forge the broker's own reports. A grant of
`$SYS/#` still reaches it, because that literal first level is not a wildcard —
the rule is about the wildcard, not about the dollar.

        raise NotImplementedError("stage 9: implement Ledger.denials()")

    def allowed(self):

        raise NotImplementedError("stage 9: implement Ledger.allowed()")

"""MQTT Broker From Scratch — stage 10: One scenario, twice, and the reader's verdict.

Nine stages have each answered one question about one packet. This one runs all
of them at once, on the world's transport, and then asks the only question that
cannot be answered by reading the code: is the broker's own account of what it did
true? A broker that believes it delivered a message the transport never carried
goes on believing it forever unless something compares the two accounts, and
nothing inside the broker can be that something — the trace it keeps and the
report it counts come from the same hand.

So the capstone is three accounts of one run. The first is the trace: every byte
the broker writes goes through `Trace.wrote` with the tick of the write, and
`read_frames` — stage 1's fixed header with stage 2's strings on top of it, the
reader the whole course has been building towards — reads that trace back with no
byte left over. A frame the reader refuses is a frame that should not have been
written. The second is the report: the thirteen counts of `REPORT_KEYS`,
recomputed from the trace, the sessions, the trie and the ledger whenever it is
asked for, never accumulated beside them. The third is the transport's own log,
which knows nothing of packets and cannot be talked into agreeing: `cross_check`
holds the numbers both accounts can state against one another and *names* the ones
that differ rather than resolving them.

A run is written as a scenario: a callable that builds its own transport, listens,
connects its clients, says their packets, and answers the broker it drove. That
shape is what makes the stage's last claim checkable — `replay` runs the scenario
again from nothing and answers the new run's bytes, and two replays of one
scenario that do not write identical bytes are proof that a `set`, an unordered
dict or a wall clock reached the wire, because a deterministic broker writing the
same packets twice has nothing else left to differ about.

    BROKER_KEYS                        the eleven fields of a run's state, in order
    REPORT_KEYS                        the thirteen counts a report carries, in order
    Trace.wrote(tick, data)            record a write at the tick it happened, answer the bytes
    Trace.frames()                     -> [(tick, bytes)], in the order they were written
    Trace.bytes()                      -> every byte the broker wrote, in order
    read_frames(data, pos=0)           -> ([(type, flags, body)], pos after the last frame)
    cross_check(report, transport)     -> {"agree": bool, "disagreements": [...]}
    replay(scenario)                   -> the bytes a fresh run of the scenario wrote
    Broker(transport, name="broker", grants=None)
    Broker.accepted()                  -> the streams that completed a CONNECT, in order
    Broker.receive(stream, data)       -> the frames written in answer to one arrival
    Broker.step(ticks=1)               -> the tick, after endings, deadlines and the flush
    Broker.report()                    -> REPORT_KEYS, counted from the trace and the sessions
    Broker.trace()                     -> the trace this broker wrote

`receive` hands back the bodies of the frames that answer the arrival being read,
and nothing else: a delivery routed to a second subscriber, a will, a re-send —
every frame the turn's caller is not the audience for — waits in its own stream's
outbound buffer and goes out on the broker's next `step`. A read that stops inside
a frame answers nothing and keeps the bytes, so the caller offers them again after
the next step and the frame is read once; a frame the course's reader refuses is
refused here, naming the bytes that arrived.

DESIGN DECISION — why is the trace read back rather than counted as it is written?
Because a counter and the thing it counts are one mistake away from disagreeing
forever. If the report were kept as running totals, every bug that wrote a frame
without counting it, or counted one it never wrote, would be invisible: the report
would be the broker's belief about itself, and a belief cannot be checked against
the thing believed. Reading the trace back with the course's own reader makes the
report a *measurement* of what was written, and it makes the reader itself part of
the test — a broker whose QoS 2 framebuilding is wrong writes a trace its own
reader refuses, and fails before any report is counted.

DESIGN DECISION — why does `cross_check` report disagreements instead of
resolving them?
Because there is nothing honest to resolve them with. The two accounts are not
the same code and cannot see the same facts: the transport knows bytes and streams
and nothing about sessions, filters or decisions, so the only keys worth comparing
are the ones both can state — the streams it opened, and the bytes it took towards
its clients. When those differ, one of the two is wrong and this function does not
know which; a resolver would have to pick, and picking the broker's own number
would make the check agree with the bug. So the answer is a verdict and a list of
name-and-both-numbers strings, and the caller decides what to do with a broker
whose account of itself is not its transport's account of it.

DESIGN DECISION — why does one turn write into two places — the caller's hand and
the stream's own buffer?
Because a turn has exactly one caller and many audiences. The frames that answer
the arrival being read go back to whoever offered those bytes, which is how a
client's own wire is kept in order without the broker stepping the clock; every
frame for anybody else has no wire to go to yet and waits for a `step` to carry

another client's wire, and a reader on the far end would then have to explain
bytes it was never meant to see — the mistake this whole course is written to
avoid, appearing in the capstone's own plumbing.

drove, and not a list of packets?
Because determinism has to be demonstrated, not promised. A scenario that rebuilds
its transport, its clients and its broker from nothing each time is the only shape
in which "the same bytes twice" is a real question: everything that could leak
across runs — a module-level cache, a dict that remembers its last iteration
order, a broker that kept a counter — is reset by construction, and `replay`
compares the two runs' writes. A scripted list of packets would prove the list is
stable, which nobody doubted, and would hide every one of those leaks.

Because MQTT has no packet that says so. There is no "your PUBLISH was refused" in
the protocol, and a broker that invented one would be writing a byte a client
could not parse; the same silence that stage 9's ledger exists to compensate for.

gets no PUBACK, a QoS 2 publish gets no PUBREC, and the client is left to
retransmit until it gives up. The alternative, acknowledging a message that was
refused, would tell the client exactly the opposite of the truth.

"""MQTT Broker From Scratch — the streams.

The world this course is handed: a transport of named, byte-oriented streams, a
clock that moves only when a caller moves it, and one ordered log that every
claim about a run can be held against. Nothing here knows what an MQTT packet is
and nothing here parses anything: the frame format is the course's own, and a
transport that framed for it would be providing the interesting half.

DESIGN DECISION — why is a stream a byte pipe rather than a message link?
Because MQTT is a byte protocol. A packet's remaining length is written into the
stream after its first byte, so a reader cannot know where a packet ends until it
has parsed that length, and the two failures worth teaching — a length split
across two arrivals, and two packets that arrive in one — cannot even be
expressed on a link that delivers whole messages. The world of
`tcp-ip-from-scratch` carries whole frames of unparsed bytes and says so; this
file is the layer above that course, where the bytes have become a stream that
may stop anywhere.

DESIGN DECISION — why does `send` return a count instead of raising?
Because a full outbox is not an error, it is backpressure. A broker that hands
the transport a 300-byte packet and gets 16 back has learned exactly what this
tick can carry, and it is the broker's own business to keep the remaining 284
bytes somewhere and try again — which is the state a real server keeps per
connection, and whose bug (forgetting the tail, or believing all 300 went) lives
until a client compares two payloads. A transport that took everything and
dropped the excess would be lying about its own name.

DESIGN DECISION — why is time a `step`, and why do the counters live here?
Because the course's claim is that a broker's honesty can be measured, and a wall
clock measures nothing: two runs of one scenario have to be the same bytes. So
time is an integer this module owns — `step(ticks)` moves it and carries one
`chunk` in each direction of every open stream — and the record of what actually
moved is kept here, in `log()` and `stats()`, recomputed from the same events
that carried the bytes. A broker that reports a delivery the transport never made
is caught by comparing the two, and that comparison means something only because
the two accounts are not the same code.

DESIGN DECISION — why can a stream be *cut* as well as closed, and why may a
stream with bytes in it not be closed at all?
Because a will is owed to a client that did not say goodbye. `close()` is an end
both sides agreed to and it refuses to happen while bytes are still in flight —
queued, carried or waiting to be taken — since an agreed end means both ends read
everything the other sent, and a client that never drained its side is the
failure this refusal names. `cut()` is the other end: nobody agreed, the peer is
gone, whatever was in flight is lost, and the loss is counted in the log rather
than quietly forgotten. A broker that only knew `close()` could not tell a client
that left politely from one that vanished, and its will would fire for both or
for neither.

The rules this module keeps, written down because they are load-bearing: every
refusal is a `StreamsError` naming the offender (the stream, the name, the count,
the byte string); `log()` and `events()` hand back copies; `to_server()`,
`to_client()` and `waiting()` are the only ways to see what arrived, and the two
`to_*` calls consume what they hand back.
"""

CHUNK = 16
BACKLOG = 4

OPEN = "open"
CLOSED = "closed"
CUT = "cut"

STATES = (OPEN, CLOSED, CUT)

EVENTS = ("listen", "connect", "accept", "send", "deliver", "close", "cut", "drop")


class StreamsError(ValueError):
    """A rule this transport cannot honour, named as the rule that is wrong."""


def _count(value, what, low=0, high=None):
    """A non-negative int in range, or a refusal naming what arrived instead."""
    if isinstance(value, bool) or not isinstance(value, int):
        raise StreamsError("%s must be an int, not %s"
                           % (what, type(value).__name__))
    if value < low or (high is not None and value > high):
        raise StreamsError("%s must be %s, not %d"
                           % (what, "at least %d" % (low,) if high is None
                              else "%d to %d" % (low, high), value))
    return value


def _bytes_of(data, what):
    """The bytes themselves, or a refusal naming the type that arrived."""
    if isinstance(data, (bytes, bytearray)):
        return bytes(data)
    raise StreamsError("%s must be bytes, not %s" % (what, type(data).__name__))


def _name(value, what):
    """A non-empty name, or a refusal naming what arrived instead."""
    if not isinstance(value, str) or not value:
        raise StreamsError("%s must be a non-empty name, not %r" % (what, value))
    return value


class Stream:
    """One connection between two names, as four buffers and a state.

    Public attributes: `id` (a small int, unique on its transport), `client` and
    `server` (the two names) and `state`, one of `STATES` — `open` only until
    somebody ends it. The buffers are the transport's business: a stage reads
    them with `to_server()` and `to_client()` and never pokes at them, which is
    what keeps `stats()` an independent account rather than a mirror.
    """

    def __init__(self, ident, client, server):
        self.id = ident
        self.client = client
        self.server = server
        self.state = OPEN
        self._queued_client = bytearray()
        self._queued_server = bytearray()
        self._arrived_server = bytearray()
        self._arrived_client = bytearray()
        self._taken_server = 0
        self._taken_client = 0

    def __repr__(self):
        return "<Stream %d %s->%s %s>" % (self.id, self.client, self.server,
                                          self.state)


class Transport:
    """The world: listeners, streams, a clock, and one log of all of it."""

    def __init__(self, rules=None):
        rules = dict(rules or {})
        for key in rules:
            if key not in ("chunk", "backlog"):
                raise StreamsError("no such rule as %r (the rules are chunk and "
                                   "backlog)" % (key,))
        self._chunk = _count(rules.get("chunk", CHUNK), "the rule 'chunk'", 1)
        self._backlog = _count(rules.get("backlog", BACKLOG), "the rule 'backlog'", 1)
        self._rules = {"chunk": self._chunk, "backlog": self._backlog}
        self._now = 0
        self._steps = 0
        self._listeners = {}
        self._streams = {}
        self._next = 1
        self._log = []

    # ---- the clock ---------------------------------------------------------

    def tick(self):
        """The current tick. Time passes only when a caller advances it."""
        return self._now

    def step(self, ticks=1):
        """Move the clock `ticks` forward, carry what fits, and return the tick.

        Each single step carries at most one `chunk` in each direction of every
        open stream, client to server first. `step(0)` is legal and carries
        nothing; a negative count is refused.
        """
        _count(ticks, "a number of ticks")
        for _ in range(ticks):
            self._now += 1
            self._steps += 1
            for stream in list(self._streams.values()):
                if stream.state == OPEN:
                    self._carry(stream)
        return self._now

    def steps(self):
        """How many single steps this transport has been moved by."""
        return self._steps

    # ---- listeners and streams ---------------------------------------------

    def listen(self, name, backlog=None):
        """Register `name` as somewhere a client may connect, and answer the name."""
        name = _name(name, "a listener's name")
        if name in self._listeners:
            raise StreamsError("a listener already answers to %r" % (name,))
        self._listeners[name] = _count(
            backlog if backlog is not None else self._backlog, "a backlog", 1)
        self._event("listen", None, name=name, backlog=self._listeners[name])
        return name

    def listeners(self):
        """The names that answer, in the order they started answering."""
        return tuple(self._listeners)

    def connect(self, client, to):
        """Open a stream from `client` to the listener `to`, and answer the stream."""
        client = _name(client, "a client's name")
        to = _name(to, "a listener's name")
        if to not in self._listeners:
            raise StreamsError("nothing listens as %r (the listeners are %r)"
                               % (to, sorted(self._listeners)))
        waiting = sum(1 for stream in self._streams.values()
                      if stream.server == to and stream.state == OPEN)
        if waiting >= self._listeners[to]:
            raise StreamsError("the backlog of %r holds %d and %d are waiting"
                               % (to, self._listeners[to], waiting))
        stream = Stream(self._next, client, to)
        self._next += 1
        self._streams[stream.id] = stream
        self._event("connect", stream)
        self._event("accept", stream)
        return stream

    def streams(self):
        """Every stream this transport has opened, in the order it made them."""
        return tuple(self._streams[key] for key in sorted(self._streams))

    def open_streams(self):
        """The streams nobody has ended yet, in the order they were connected."""
        return tuple(stream for stream in self.streams() if stream.state == OPEN)

    def stream(self, ident):
        """The stream with this id (or this `Stream`), or a refusal naming the id."""
        if isinstance(ident, Stream):
            return self.stream(ident.id)
        if isinstance(ident, bool) or not isinstance(ident, int):
            raise StreamsError("a stream id must be an int, not %s"
                               % (type(ident).__name__,))
        if ident not in self._streams:
            raise StreamsError("no stream %d (the streams are %r)"
                               % (ident, sorted(self._streams)))
        return self._streams[ident]

    # ---- bytes: the client's direction -------------------------------------

    def send(self, stream, data):
        """The client's bytes towards the server, and how many of them were taken.

        What does not fit stays in the caller's hands: nothing is ever queued
        beyond the outbox's own room, so a short answer is the truth about this
        tick. The transport never drops what it took; it only takes what it can
        carry next step.
        """
        stream = self.stream(stream)
        if stream.state != OPEN:
            raise StreamsError("stream %d is %s and carries nothing"
                               % (stream.id, stream.state))
        data = _bytes_of(data, "the bytes a stream carries")
        room = self._chunk - len(stream._queued_client)
        taken = min(room, len(data))
        if taken:
            stream._queued_client += data[:taken]
            self._event("send", stream, side="server", count=taken)
        return taken

    def to_server(self, stream):
        """Everything the client's bytes have become at the server, and take it."""
        stream = self.stream(stream)
        arrived = bytes(stream._arrived_server)
        stream._arrived_server.clear()
        if arrived:
            stream._taken_server += len(arrived)
        return arrived

    # ---- bytes: the server's direction -------------------------------------

    def answer(self, stream, data):
        """The server's bytes towards the client, and how many of them were taken.

        The same contract as `send`, in the other direction: a short answer is
        backpressure, and the tail is the broker's to hold or lose.
        """
        stream = self.stream(stream)
        if stream.state != OPEN:
            raise StreamsError("stream %d is %s and carries nothing"
                               % (stream.id, stream.state))
        data = _bytes_of(data, "the bytes a stream carries")
        room = self._chunk - len(stream._queued_server)
        taken = min(room, len(data))
        if taken:
            stream._queued_server += data[:taken]
            self._event("send", stream, side="client", count=taken)
        return taken

    def to_client(self, stream):
        """Everything the server's bytes have become at the client, and take it."""
        stream = self.stream(stream)
        arrived = bytes(stream._arrived_client)
        stream._arrived_client.clear()
        if arrived:
            stream._taken_client += len(arrived)
        return arrived

    def waiting(self, stream):
        """The bytes in flight for each end, as `(to_server, to_client)`.

        A read: what has been queued or carried and not yet taken, in both
        directions, without taking any of it.
        """
        stream = self.stream(stream)
        return (len(stream._queued_client) + len(stream._arrived_server),
                len(stream._queued_server) + len(stream._arrived_client))

    def waiting_at(self, stream, end):
        """The bytes in flight for one end: `"server"` or `"client"`."""
        if end not in ("server", "client"):
            raise StreamsError("an end is 'server' or 'client', not %r" % (end,))
        queued, arrived = self.waiting(stream)
        return queued if end == "server" else arrived

    # ---- endings -----------------------------------------------------------

    def close(self, stream):
        """End a stream both sides agreed to; refuses while bytes are in flight.

        An agreed end means both ends read everything the other sent. A stream
        with bytes queued, carried or waiting to be taken is refused by name,
        because closing it would leave somebody's bytes in a buffer nobody will
        ever read.
        """
        stream = self.stream(stream)
        if stream.state != OPEN:
            raise StreamsError("stream %d is already %s" % (stream.id, stream.state))
        queued = len(stream._queued_client) + len(stream._queued_server)
        arrived = len(stream._arrived_server) + len(stream._arrived_client)
        if queued or arrived:
            raise StreamsError("stream %d still holds %d bytes in flight (%d "
                               "queued, %d arrived and untaken)"
                               % (stream.id, queued + arrived, queued, arrived))
        stream.state = CLOSED
        self._event("close", stream)
        return stream

    def cut(self, stream, reason="the peer is gone"):
        """End a stream nobody agreed to: what was in flight is lost and counted."""
        stream = self.stream(stream)
        if stream.state != OPEN:
            raise StreamsError("stream %d is already %s" % (stream.id, stream.state))
        _name(reason, "the reason a stream was cut")
        lost = (len(stream._queued_client) + len(stream._queued_server)
                + len(stream._arrived_server) + len(stream._arrived_client))
        stream.state = CUT
        self._event("cut", stream, reason=reason, lost=lost)
        if lost:
            self._event("drop", stream, count=lost)
        return stream

    # ---- the record --------------------------------------------------------

    def log(self):
        """Every event this transport saw, in order: copies, not a live view."""
        return [dict(record) for record in self._log]

    def events(self, event):
        """One kind of event, in order."""
        if event not in EVENTS:
            raise StreamsError("no such event as %r (the events are %r)"
                               % (event, EVENTS))
        return [dict(record) for record in self._log if record["event"] == event]

    def stats(self):
        """The counts, recomputed from the log rather than accumulated beside it."""
        counts = {event: 0 for event in EVENTS}
        for record in self._log:
            counts[record["event"]] += 1
        return {
            "ticks": self._now,
            "steps": self._steps,
            "listeners": len(self._listeners),
            "streams": len(self._streams),
            "connects": counts["connect"],
            "accepts": counts["accept"],
            "closes": counts["close"],
            "cuts": counts["cut"],
            "sends": counts["send"],
            "delivers": counts["deliver"],
            "takes": sum(stream._taken_server + stream._taken_client
                         for stream in self._streams.values()),
            "bytes_sent": sum(record["count"] for record in self._log
                              if record["event"] == "send"),
            "bytes_carried": sum(record["count"] for record in self._log
                                 if record["event"] == "deliver"),
            "bytes_dropped": sum(record["count"] for record in self._log
                                 if record["event"] == "drop"),
            "chunk": self._chunk,
            "backlog": self._backlog,
        }

    def rules(self):
        """The rules this transport was built with, as they were given."""
        return dict(self._rules)

    def reset(self):
        """Forget the streams, the listeners, the log and the counts; keep the clock."""
        self._streams = {}
        self._listeners = {}
        self._log = []
        self._next = 1

    # ---- the private half --------------------------------------------------

    def _carry(self, stream):
        """Move one `chunk` of each queue across, and log the two arrivals."""
        for queued, arrived, side in (
                (stream._queued_client, stream._arrived_server, "server"),
                (stream._queued_server, stream._arrived_client, "client")):
            moved = min(self._chunk, len(queued))
            if not moved:
                continue
            arrived += queued[:moved]
            del queued[:moved]
            self._event("deliver", stream, side=side, count=moved)

    def _event(self, event, stream, **fields):
        record = {"tick": self._now, "event": event,
                  "stream": None if stream is None else stream.id}
        record.update(fields)
        self._log.append(record)
        return record

"""The tiny API an authored course uses to describe its stages.

A course is a directory containing `course.py`:

    from codecraft.api import stage

    TITLE = "Build a Bloom Filter"
    DESCRIPTION = "A probabilistic set, from hashing to false-positive math."

    def check_1():
        from bloom import BloomFilter
        bf = BloomFilter(bits=64, hashes=2)
        bf.add("x")
        assert "x" in bf
        assert "y" not in bf, "a fresh filter must not report false members"

    STAGES = [
        stage(
            1,
            file="bloom.py",
            title="add and contains",
            tags=["hashing", "data-structure"],
            action="Implement add() to set the k bit positions.",
            predict="can contains() ever be certain an item is absent?",
            hints=["bits = bits[:] to avoid shared state",
                   "use one hash salt per position"],
            check=check_1,
        ),
        ...
    ]

`codecraft run <course>` imports this file, runs each `check`, records the
attempt, and hands the result to the adaptive engine. `hints` are optional —
when omitted, the engine generates them from `action`/`predict`.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Optional


@dataclass
class Stage:
    id: int
    file: str
    title: str
    check: Callable[[], None]
    tags: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    action: str = ""
    predict: str = ""
    hints: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    solution: Optional[str] = None   # e.g. "solutions/bloom.py: BloomFilter.add"

    def meta(self) -> Dict[str, object]:
        return {
            "file": self.file,
            "title": self.title,
            "tags": list(self.tags),
            "action": self.action,
            "predict": self.predict,
            "hints": list(self.hints),
            "solution": self.solution,
        }


def stage(id: int, file: str, title: str, check: Callable[[], None],
          tags: Optional[List[str]] = None, action: str = "", predict: str = "",
          hints: Optional[List[str]] = None,
          solution: Optional[str] = None) -> Stage:
    """Convenience constructor so course.py stays readable."""
    return Stage(
        id=id, file=file, title=title, check=check, tags=list(tags or []),
        action=action, predict=predict, hints=list(hints or []),
        solution=solution,
    )
